title: Naim Montazeri, Ph.D.
text:
I am an Assistant Professor at the University of Florida with over 15 years of experience in microbial food safety, risk assessment, and predictive modeling. My work integrates experimental microbiology with R-based data analysis to evaluate pathogen persistence, transfer, and control in foods and agricultural systems, with particular experience in high-risk ready-to-eat foods, agricultural water, and risk-based strategies that support food safety decision-making and regulatory compliance. I also have experience applying FDA BAM, ISO, ASTM, AOAC, and EPA-aligned methods in food safety, sanitation, and validation studies.
My work is cross-functional, combining microbiology, data analysis, applied food safety, stakeholder outreach, science communication, and mentoring. Prior to my current role, I worked on sanitation validation, product development, processing, and quality evaluation in laboratory and pilot-scale environments, including antimicrobial interventions, thermal processing, sensory quality, and product stability.

title: Microbial Thermal Inactivation and Risk-Based Modeling
text:
Project Summary
Developed and validated kinetic and dynamic models to quantify thermal inactivation of bacteria (Vibrio parahaemolyticus) and viruses (human norovirus) in high-risk foods, including oysters. Applied R-based linear and non-linear modeling, Monte Carlo simulation, and uncertainty analysis to estimate key inactivation parameters such as D- and z-values. These predictive models support risk-based process validation and inform cooking recommendations. This work supports development of validated time–temperature controls for high-risk foods.

title: Microbial Thermal Inactivation and Risk-Based Modeling
text:
Why It Matters
Thermal process validation for high-risk foods often relies on bacterial indicators that may not accurately represent viral behavior. This work addresses this limitation by integrating experimental data with predictive modeling to characterize microbial inactivation under realistic processing conditions.
In parallel, survey data collected from U.S. restaurants on oyster cooking practices (see study) were used to inform model inputs and validate assumptions against real-world conditions. This ensures the resulting recommendations are directly applicable to industry practices rather than idealized laboratory scenarios.

title: Microbial Thermal Inactivation and Risk-Based Modeling
text:
Key Contributions

Developed kinetic and dynamic inactivation models for bacteria and viruses
Applied R-based modeling, Monte Carlo simulation, and uncertainty analysis, with workflows and data deposited in public repositories
Estimated key parameters including D- and z-values
Supported validation of time–temperature combinations for high-risk foods

title: Agricultural Water Treatment and FSMA Compliance
text:
Project Summary
Evaluated sanitizer efficacy in preharvest agricultural water collected from Florida farms under realistic conditions. Verified performance of chlorine-based sanitizers across different contact times, temperatures, and sanitizer concentrations. Applied kinetic modeling to estimate the treatment conditions required to achieve FSMA’s 3-log microbial reduction target, supporting risk-based water management decisions for produce safety. In related work, evaluated novel treatment approaches such as chitosan microparticles, which reduced microbial loads in fecally polluted water by up to 2 log.

title: Agricultural Water Treatment and FSMA Compliance
text:
Why It Matters
Agricultural water quality varies substantially across production environments, which directly affects treatment efficacy and food safety outcomes. This work addresses that challenge by evaluating microbial control strategies under realistic water conditions rather than idealized laboratory matrices.
The results are directly relevant to produce operations and regulatory compliance, as they identify treatment conditions required to achieve FSMA-aligned microbial reduction targets under variable field conditions. This supports validation of agricultural water treatment strategies and implementation of risk-based preventive controls.
In multiple cases, viral targets demonstrated greater resistance than bacterial indicators under comparable treatment conditions, highlighting limitations of indicator-based validation approaches. This underscores the importance of integrating experimental data with kinetic modeling to inform risk-based water management decisions that account for variability in microbial responses.

title: Agricultural Water Treatment and FSMA Compliance
text:
Key Contributions

Evaluated sanitizer efficacy in agricultural water collected from commercial farm environments
Quantified treatment performance across different contact times, temperatures, and concentrations
Applied kinetic modeling to estimate treatment conditions required to achieve FSMA’s 3-log microbial reduction target
Assessed novel mitigation approaches, including chitosan microparticles, for microbial reduction in fecally polluted water
Generated data to support risk-based agricultural water management decisions
